lines.trans: Why does he not want me?
Because you turned him down. He is under stress.
When I yell at Senya, he cannot do anything for a week afterward.
He is stressed, and I am the one suffering.
You need to help him relax.
How about arranging a romantic evening?
A bubble bath, candles, music.
He comes home, and you stand up like that,
walk up to him, and take his face in your hands.
Anyway, Kostya is working the night shift on room service tonight.
I will go stay with a friend.
The apartment is at your disposal.
You can do it everywhere.
Except on my bed, of course.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'чему').

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?
Why are you here?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Grab him!
It needs a wash.
Four-eyes! Grab him!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'me', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'wants', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You're greedy!
Have you got any more?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'refused / turned down', paired with 'отказывать'.

examples.text: Марина, послушайте, это я вам отказал!
examples.trans: Marina, listen, I was the one who turned you down!
They turned him down in court.

examples.text: Я мерзкий? Марина, послушайте, это я вам отказал!
examples.trans: I'm disgusting? Marina, listen, I was the one who turned you down!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, near, with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ой, кажется, у вас сломан нос!
examples.trans: Oh, it looks like your nose is broken!

examples.text: Завтра у меня важное собеседование на работу.
examples.trans: Tomorrow I have an important job interview.

examples.text: Значит, у нас с тобой много общего.
examples.trans: So you and I have a lot in common.

meanings.note: 20th-century borrowing from English 'stress' (ultimately from Old French 'estrece', narrowness/oppression).

examples.trans: Any stress and it will be bad.

examples.text: Я не могу работать в таком стрессе.
examples.trans: I cannot work in such stress.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'here, there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There, look.
Here's my toy car.
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'орать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'I yell at'.

related.gloss: not to I yell at (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и наорать вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and I yell at on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют наорать.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to I yell at.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'then, afterwards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: First coffee, then work.
I'll call later.
And then waste will flow.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'деля'). Common feminine noun meaning 'week' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I've been waiting a week.
The sea in a week!

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's nothing left.
I don't know anything.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'maybe', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Maybe tomorrow.
I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'I suffer / torment myself'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и мучиться вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and I suffer on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют мучиться.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to I suffer.

meanings.en: it is necessary, one needs to
meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to make a call.
You need to rest.

examples.text: Мне нужно позвонить губернатору. Дай телефон.
examples.trans: I need to call the governor. Give me a phone.

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'слабить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to relax', paired with 'расслаблять'.

examples.text: Но доктор сказал расслабить твои мышцы!
examples.trans: But the doctor said to relax your muscles!
A warm bath helps relax the muscles.

meanings.en: to arrange, organize, set up an event or scheme
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'строить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'let us arrange', paired with 'устраивать'.

examples.text: Я всё устрою на высшем уровне.
examples.trans: I will arrange everything at the highest level.
They organized a party for friends.
To cause disturbances.

meanings.note: Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('romantic').

examples.text: Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.
This is a very romantic place.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'evening' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Good evening!
I'll call in the evening.

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'bathtub / bath' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The carp live in the bathtub.
They live wonderfully in the bathtub.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with / from', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'with foam / bubbles' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I need shaving foam.

examples.text: Сеня, ты скоро? Мне нужна пена!
examples.trans: Senya, are you nearly done? I need the foam!
I need the foam!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'веча'). Common feminine noun meaning 'candles' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я приношу бутылку шампанского и свечи.
examples.trans: I'll bring a bottle of champagne and candles.
Candles are burning on the table.

examples.text: Прекрасно! Я приношу бутылку шампанского и свечи.
examples.trans: Wonderful! I'll bring a bottle of champagne and candles.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'music' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: We'll find some music right now.
I like listening to quiet music.

examples.text: Вань, посмотри! — Смотри, работает! Сейчас музыку найдём.
examples.trans: Vanya, look! — Look, it works! We'll find some music right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'comes', paired with 'прийти'.

examples.trans: Come tomorrow.
He comes every day.
If you change your mind, come back. The job is waiting.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('so').

examples.trans: What is this?
He's so kind.
Pavel Yuryevich, what is this?

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'тавать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'you stand up', paired with 'встать'.

examples.trans: Come on, Tuzik, let's get up!
I get up at seven in the morning.
Come on, Tuzik, let's get up!

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'you walk up', paired with 'подойти'.

examples.trans: Let's go, our turn in the queue is coming up.
The train is approaching the station.

examples.text: Я к печке подхожу. А он маячит перед глазами!
examples.trans: I walk up to the stove. And it dangles right before my eyes!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'to, towards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.
I'm going to Mum's.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'do you take/get', paired with 'взять'.

examples.trans: We have to take all the money.
He doesn't take bribes.
I'm not taking the knife.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'face' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It really suits you!
He has a very kind face.

examples.text: Карамельно-сливочный цвет. Очень тебе к лицу! Надень куртку.
examples.trans: A caramel-cream colour. It really suits you! Put the jacket on.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'long story short', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Long story short, no.
Basically, I don't know.

examples.text: Короче, Самсон, сегодня ты приводишь её к Димону.
examples.trans: In short, Samson, tonight you bring her to Dimon's place.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'егодня').

examples.trans: I'm at home today.
I'll be there tonight.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('night').

examples.text: Шеф говорит, что это очень ночной выбор.
examples.trans: The chef says that this is a very night choice.

examples.text: У нас сегодня просто ночной день в ресторане.
examples.trans: We are having a simply night day at the restaurant today.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мена'). Common feminine noun meaning 'shift' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: We're on the afternoon shift today.
His shift has ended.

examples.text: А у нас сегодня вторая смена.
examples.trans: We're on the afternoon shift today.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'room service' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть рум-сервис.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always room service.
The chef immediately noticed where the room service was.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'руга'). Common feminine noun meaning 'to a female friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I'll invite a female friend over.
She is my best friend.

examples.text: Пять тысяч рублей. Я подругу приглашу.
examples.trans: Five thousand roubles. I'll invite a female friend over.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will go', paired with 'идти'.

examples.trans: May I go?
Let's go home.
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'flat, apartment' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is my flat.
We live in a flat.
Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is your coffee.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
Your boss is here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'поряжение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'disposal' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Victoria Sergeyevna's order, chef.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть распоряжение.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always disposal.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'делать'.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
I'll do it tomorrow.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'everywhere', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's water everywhere!
I looked everywhere.
Vanya, the water! There's water everywhere!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'except', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ни у кого в городе нет денег, кроме Игнатьева.
examples.trans: Nobody in town has any money, except Ignatyev.
Everyone came except him.
I am speaking seriously, no joking!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
That's mine.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'bed' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is my bed.
Foot on the bed.

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Of course I'll help.
Yes, of course.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?
